steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on a federated XGBoost method for the horizontal setting that avoids sharing gradients and hessians by making the learning rates of the aggregated trees learnable. It should motivate the problem, explain what is wrong with existing approaches, and list our contributions.

- Our idea: learnable learning rates, no gradient sharing

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- FL and its focus on NN
  - global model from decentralized data, privacy-preserving, vs. centralized training
  - existing FL research and techniques (convergence, privacy risks, costs) mostly on neural networks
  - other ML models under-explored
- XGBoost and need for federated XGBoost
  - EXtreme Gradient Boosting: powerful, interpretable GBDT
  - beats deep learning on tabular data, medium-sized datasets under 10k examples, in most cases
  - cross-silo FL: 2 to 100 organizations
  - tasks: survival analysis, financial fraud detection
- Two settings (Fig. 1)
  - horizontal: same feature spaces, different sample IDs; server sends global model, aggregates updated params each round
  - vertical: first proposed by SecureBoost; passive parties + one active party; same sample space, different features; active party has labels -> acts as server
- Horizontal is harder
  - more common, but harder to train
  - optimal split condition depends on order of data samples (iterate features, partition left/right)
  - vertical: same sample IDs -> passive parties just send sample order
  - horizontal: different IDs -> at every split each client sends gradients, hessians and/or sample splits
  - problem 1: per-node level communication frequency; depth L, M trees; up to M\times 2^{L} nodes = rounds; depth 8, 500 trees -> \sim 100K rounds; possibly more than one round per node + cryptographic calculations
  - problem 2: serious privacy concerns; sharing gradients / confident info insecure; training data can be reconstructed from gradients
- Existing horizontal work: privacy vs. communication trade-off
  - FedXGB: secure aggregation with homomorphic encryption + secret sharing; high overhead at per-node frequency
  - gradient histograms: quantile sketch, faster, but frequency tied to tree depth; still leak (bins, thresholds inferred)
  - obfuscation: clustering-based k-anonymity, locality-sensitive hashing; less overhead than encryption, but performance vs. number of clients trade-off
- Our approach
  - question: federated XGBoost in horizontal setting without sharing gradients and hessians?
  - boosts privacy + disentangles per-node communication frequency
  - intuition: heterogeneous local data -> fixed learning rate per tree too weak (different mistakes under distribution shift)
  - learnable learning rates via small one-layer 1D CNN, kernel size and stride = number of trees per client ensemble; prediction outcomes as inputs
  - clients send only tree ensembles

  - FedXGBllr (federated XGBoost with learnable learning rates), horizontal, no gradients/hessians

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Federated Learning (FL) lets us train a global model on decentralized datasets while keeping privacy, which is different from the usual centralized way of training. Most FL research and the techniques that were developed to make models converge better and to reduce privacy risks and costs are focused on neural networks (NN). Developing FL algorithms for other machine learning (ML) models has not been explored much.

EXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) is a gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) that is powerful and also interpretable. For tabular data on medium-sized datasets with under 10k training examples, XGBoost beats deep learning methods in most cases. In cross-silo FL the pool of clients is usually 2 to 100 organizations, and there is a growing need for a federated XGBoost system for tasks like survival analysis and financial fraud detection.

There are two settings that existing works on federated XGBoost usually follow (Fig. 1). In the horizontal setting the clients' datasets have the same feature spaces but different sample IDs. The central server sends the global model to all the clients and then it aggregates the updated model parameters after each communication round. The vertical setting was first proposed by SecureBoost. It introduced passive parties and one active party, which share the same sample space but have different features. Only the active party owns the data labels, so it acts as the server.

The horizontal setting is more common, but training a horizontal federated XGBoost is actually harder. This is because finding the optimal split condition of XGBoost trees depends on the order of the data samples, since we iterate over the feature set and partition the samples into left and right based on the feature constraints. In the vertical setting all clients share the same sample IDs, so the passive parties only have to send the order of the samples to the active party. In the horizontal setting the sample IDs are different across clients, so at every splitting point each client has to send the gradients, hessians, and/or sample splits based on the feature values to the server so it can find the optimal splitting condition. This vanilla approach has two key problems.

- 1. Per-node level communication frequency. The server has to communicate with all the clients at every splitting point. Let L be the depth of each tree and M the number of trees in the ensemble. The number of nodes in the ensemble can scale up to M\times 2^{L}, and the number of communication rounds scales the same way. A trained XGBoost model commonly has a depth of 8 and 500 trees, so the number of communication rounds can reach \sim 100K. Also, in a real application the server may do more than one round of communication per node and do extra cryptographic calculations. So the communication overhead is high and this makes horizontal federated XGBoost hard to deploy in practice.

- 2. Serious privacy concerns. Sharing gradients and even confident information was shown to be insecure in distributed training of ML models. The training data can be reconstructed from gradients, so this sharing has to be protected.

- Existing horizontal work: privacy vs. communication trade-off
  - FedXGB: homomorphic encryption + secret sharing on shared parameters, high overhead at per-node frequency
  - gradient histograms / quantile sketch: faster, but communication still tied to tree depth; bins and thresholds can be inferred
  - clustering-based k-anonymity, locality-sensitive hashing: less overhead than encryption, but trade-off between performance and number of clients
- Our approach
  - can we avoid sharing gradients and hessians in the horizontal setting?
  - intuition: heterogeneous clients -> fixed learning rate per tree too weak
  - learnable learning rates: small one-layer 1D CNN, kernel size and stride = number of trees per client ensemble, prediction outcomes as inputs
  - clients only send tree ensembles; rounds independent of XGBoost hyperparameters; 10 rounds enough
  - overhead independent of dataset size, lower by tens to hundreds
- Contributions
  - FedXGBllr; disentangled communication frequency; 25x to 700x lower overhead; interpretable; classification and regression experiments; released under Flower

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Federated Learning (FL) lets us train a global model on decentralized datasets while keeping privacy, which is different from the usual centralized way of training. Most FL research and the techniques that were developed to make models converge better and to reduce privacy risks and costs are focused on neural networks (NN). Developing FL algorithms for other machine learning (ML) models has not been explored much.

EXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) is a gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT) that is powerful and also interpretable. For tabular data on medium-sized datasets with under 10k training examples, XGBoost beats deep learning methods in most cases. In cross-silo FL the pool of clients is usually 2 to 100 organizations, and there is a growing need for a federated XGBoost system for tasks like survival analysis and financial fraud detection.

There are two settings that existing works on federated XGBoost usually follow (Fig. 1). In the horizontal setting the clients' datasets have the same feature spaces but different sample IDs. The central server sends the global model to all the clients and then it aggregates the updated model parameters after each communication round. The vertical setting was first proposed by SecureBoost. It introduced passive parties and one active party, which share the same sample space but have different features. Only the active party owns the data labels, so it acts as the server.

The horizontal setting is more common, but training a horizontal federated XGBoost is actually harder. This is because finding the optimal split condition of XGBoost trees depends on the order of the data samples, since we iterate over the feature set and partition the samples into left and right based on the feature constraints. In the vertical setting all clients share the same sample IDs, so the passive parties only have to send the order of the samples to the active party. In the horizontal setting the sample IDs are different across clients, so at every splitting point each client has to send the gradients, hessians, and/or sample splits based on the feature values to the server so it can find the optimal splitting condition. This vanilla approach has two key problems.

- 1. Per-node level communication frequency. The server has to communicate with all the clients at every splitting point. Let L be the depth of each tree and M the number of trees in the ensemble. The number of nodes in the ensemble can scale up to M\times 2^{L}, and the number of communication rounds scales the same way. A trained XGBoost model commonly has a depth of 8 and 500 trees, so the number of communication rounds can reach \sim 100K. Also, in a real application the server may do more than one round of communication per node and do extra cryptographic calculations. So the communication overhead is high and this makes horizontal federated XGBoost hard to deploy in practice.

- 2. Serious privacy concerns. Sharing gradients and even confident information was shown to be insecure in distributed training of ML models. The training data can be reconstructed from gradients, so this sharing has to be protected.

Existing research on horizontal federated XGBoost deals with these two problems by trading off privacy against communication costs. Some works use stronger defenses against privacy leaks. FedXGB made a new secure aggregation protocol that applies homomorphic encryption and secret sharing directly on the shared parameters. But this causes high communication and computation overhead, at per-node level communication frequency. Other works lower the resolution of the raw data distribution by making a surrogate representation with gradient histograms. Histogram-based methods make training faster by building a quantile sketch approximation, but the communication frequency is still tied to the depth of the trees. They can also still leak privacy because the gradients related to the bins and the thresholds can be inferred. There are also works that obfuscate the raw data distribution with methods like clustering-based k-anonymity and locality-sensitive hashing. They need less communication overhead than encryption-based methods, but there is a trade-off between model performance and the number of clients.

In this work we ask a basic question: is it possible to build a federated XGBoost in the horizontal setting without sharing gradients and hessians? If it is, we could improve privacy and also disentangle the per-node level communication frequency at the same time. We find that it is possible, based on an intuition: the clients' local datasets can be heterogeneous in the horizontal setting, so a fixed learning rate for each tree may be too weak, because each tree can make different amounts of mistakes on unseen data with distribution shifts. So we make the learning rates of the aggregated tree ensembles learnable, by training a small one-layer 1D CNN whose kernel size and stride are equal to the number of trees in each client tree ensemble. The prediction outcomes are used directly as inputs. This framework preserves privacy. Clients only send the constructed tree ensemble to the server, and gradients and hessians, which may leak sensitive information, do not need to be shared. Also, the number of communication rounds does not depend on any hyperparameter of the trained XGBoost. In practice 10 communication rounds are enough for the global federated XGBoost model to reach performance comparable to the state-of-the-art method. The total communication overhead for training the global model also does not depend on the dataset size. Our approach has total communication overhead lower than previous works in the order of tens to hundreds.

Our main contributions are:

- We propose FedXGBllr, a new privacy-preserving framework. It is a federated XGBoost with learnable learning rates in the horizontal setting and it does not rely on sharing gradients and hessians.

- Our framework disentangles the per-node level communication frequency when training a federated XGBoost.

- The total communication overhead of our framework does not depend on the dataset size and is much lower (by factors from 25x to 700x) than previous methods.

- We show that FedXGBllr is interpretable, with reasoning and analysis.

- We do extensive experiments on classification and regression datasets with different feature dimensions and sizes. Our results are comparable to the state-of-the-art horizontal federated XGBoost.

- The implementation is released under Flower, a comprehensive, end-to-end FL framework.

steps.text:
Federated Learning (FL) enables training a global model using decentralized datasets in a privacy-preserving manner, in contrast with the conventional centralized training paradigm [1,2,3,4,5]. Existing FL research [6,7,8,9] and the techniques developed [10,11,12,13] to optimize model convergence and reduce systematic privacy risks and costs mainly focus on neural networks (NN). The efforts to develop FL algorithms that support other machine learning (ML) models, on the other hand, remain under-explored.

EXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) [14] is a powerful and interpretable gradient-boosted decision tree (GBDT). In most cases, XGBoost outperforms deep learning methods for tabular data on medium-sized datasets under 10k training examples [15,16,17]. In the context of cross-silo FL, where the client pool is typically made up of 2 to 100 [10] organizations, there is a growing need to deploy a federated XGBoost system on specific tasks such as survival analysis [18] and financial fraud detection [19,20].

Existing works on federated XGBoost usually follow two settings (Fig. 1). The horizontal setting is the case where clients' datasets have identical feature spaces but different sample IDs. The central server sends the global model to all clients and then aggregates the updated model parameters after each communication round. In the vertical setting, first proposed by SecureBoost [19,21], the concepts of passive parties and one active party were introduced, where passive parties and the active party share an identical sample space but possess different features. As only the active party owns data labels, it naturally acts as the server.

Although the horizontal setting is more common [22], training a horizontal federated XGBoost turns out to be harder, not easier, because finding the optimal split condition of XGBoost trees depends on the order of the data samples [23,24] as we iterate the feature set and partition the data samples into left and right according to the feature constraints. As all clients share the same sample IDs in the vertical setting, the passive parties only need to send the order of the samples to the active party. However, since the sample IDs differ across clients in the horizontal setting, at every splitting point each client needs to transmit the gradients, hessians, and/or sample splits based on the feature values to the server to find the optimal splitting condition [25]. Hence, we identify two key problems with this vanilla approach.

- 1. Per-node level communication frequency. The server needs to communicate with all clients at every splitting point. We denote the depth of each tree as L and the number of trees in the tree ensemble as M. The number of nodes in the tree ensemble can scale up to M\times 2^{L} [26], and so can the number of communication rounds. As it is common for a trained XGBoost model to have a depth of 8 and 500 trees [14], the number of communication rounds can reach \sim 100K. Moreover, in a real application of federated XGBoost, the server may conduct more than one round of communication per node [27] and carry out extra cryptographic calculations. The high communication overhead thus makes it difficult to deploy horizontal federated XGBoost for practical uses.

- 2. Serious privacy concerns. Sharing gradients and even confident information was proved to be insecure in the distributed training of ML models [28,29]. As the training data can be reconstructed from gradients, such sharing needs to be protected.

Existing research on horizontal federated XGBoost tackles these two problems by seeking a trade-off between privacy and communication costs. A few works take stronger defenses against privacy leaks. FedXGB [27] developed a new secure aggregation protocol by applying homomorphic encryption and secret sharing directly on shared parameters. However, this induces high communication and computation overhead at per-node level communication frequency. Some works decrease the resolution of the raw data distribution by generating a surrogate representation using gradient histograms [23,26,22,25]. Histogram-based methods accelerate training by building a quantile sketch approximation, but the communication frequency still correlates with the depth of the trees. Besides, they can still leak privacy because the gradients related to the bins and the thresholds can be inferred [30]. Other works obfuscate the raw data distribution with methods including clustering-based k-anonymity [31] and locality-sensitive hashing [32]. Although they require less communication overhead than encryption-based methods, these approaches trade off model performance against the number of clients.

In this work, we ask a fundamental question: is it possible to construct a federated XGBoost in the horizontal setting without relying on the sharing of gradients and hessians? This way, we could simultaneously boost privacy and disentangle the per-node level communication frequency. We find it to be possible by formulating an important intuition: as the local datasets of clients can be heterogeneous in the horizontal setting, a fixed learning rate for each tree may be too weak, since each tree can make different amounts of mistakes on unseen data with distribution shifts. To this end, we make the learning rates of the aggregated tree ensembles learnable by training a small one-layer 1D CNN with kernel size and stride equal to the number of trees in each client tree ensemble, using the prediction outcomes directly as inputs. This novel framework preserves privacy: the clients only need to send the constructed tree ensemble to the server, and the sharing of gradients and hessians, which may leak sensitive information, is not required. In addition, the number of communication rounds is independent of any hyperparameter related to the trained XGBoost. In practice, we find 10 communication rounds sufficient for the global federated XGBoost model to reach performance comparable to the state-of-the-art method. Moreover, the total communication overhead of training a global federated XGBoost model is independent of the dataset size, and is lower than that of previous works in the order of tens to hundreds.

The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows:

- • We propose a novel privacy-preserving framework, FedXGBllr, a federated XGBoost with learnable learning rates in the horizontal setting that does not rely on the sharing of gradients and hessians.

- • Our framework disentangles the per-node level communication frequency when training a federated XGBoost.

- • The total communication overhead of our framework is independent of the dataset size and is significantly lower (by factors from 25x to 700x) than previous methods.

- • We show that FedXGBllr is interpretable with carefully framed reasoning and analysis.

- • We conduct extensive experiments on classification and regression datasets with diverse feature dimensions and sizes. Our results are comparable to the state-of-the-art horizontal federated XGBoost.

- • The implementation is released under Flower [33], a comprehensive, end-to-end FL framework.
